title: NExT-Guard: Training-Free Streaming Safeguard without Token-Level Labels
claim: Prior safeguards need token-level supervised training and overfit to surface semantics; ours reuses any post-hoc guard via SAE features and flags the right tokens.
layout: 4 panels, stacked top-to-bottom in red (prior) and blue (ours) zones, with example text
description: The figure has two stacked rounded regions. The top region has a pink tint and covers the current paradigm. Panel (a) shows a row of token capsules for the LLM's generation process, with the unsafe token shaded orange-purple and future tokens crossed out in a dashed box. A red dashed box labelled 'token-level safety supervision' feeds a red 'Supervised Training for Streaming Guard' box, which outputs [Safe] and [Unsafe]. Panel (b), 'Limitation: Overfitting', shows two example sentences. The word 'Kill' in a benign Python command is highlighted red and marked with a red X, and a harmful sentence is also marked with an X. The bottom region has a light blue tint. Panel (c), 'NExT-Guard (Ours)', has the same token row, but the blue box reads 'Any Post-hoc Safeguard' and a dashed 'decomposing by SAE' inset shows safe and unsafe bars. Panel (d), 'Precisely Intervention', shows the same sentences with only 'forever' highlighted blue and check marks. The eye goes first to the red-versus-blue contrast.
caption: Comparison between current streaming safety and NExT-Guard. (a) Current paradigm relies heavily on token-level labels. (b) Qwen3-Guard-8B-Streaming [ref] is prone to severe overfitting to individual token semantics. (c) NExT-Guard achieves streaming safety without training. (d) Unsafe tokens are precisely identified by NExT-Guard. Best viewed in color.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in streaming scenarios, rendering conventional post-hoc safeguards ineffective as they fail to interdict unsafe content in real-time. While streaming safeguards based on token-level supervised training could address this, they necessitate expensive annotations and suffer from severe overfitting. In this work, we challenge the paradigm that streaming safety must rely on token-level supervised training. Instead, it is an inherent capability of well-trained post-hoc safeguards, as they already encode token-level risk signals in hidden representations. Hence, we introduce NExT-Guard, a training-free framework that achieves streaming safeguards by monitoring interpretable latent features from Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). It uses pretrained SAEs from publicly available base LLMs, enabling flexible, low-cost deployment without token-level supervision. Experimental results show that NExT-Guard outperforms both post-hoc and streaming safeguards based on supervised training, with superior robustness across models, SAE variants, and risk scenarios. These results make NExT-Guard a universal and scalable paradigm for real-time safety, accelerating the practical deployment of streaming safeguards.
